content: The quality of data regarding the administration of the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine needs to be improved. The birth dose should be followed by two or three additional doses to complete the primary vaccination series. Tenofovir prophylaxis is recommended to prevent mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus (HBV). Women who are co-infected with HIV and HBV should receive antiretroviral therapy (ART) based on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), which also serves as prophylaxis against HBV transmission to the child. This is in addition to the three-dose HBV vaccination schedule for all infants, which includes a timely birth dose. This recommendation is conditional and supported by moderate-certainty evidence. In settings where the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the general population is ≥2% or ≥5%, it is recommended that all adults and adolescents have routine access to HBsAg serological testing. This testing should be linked to prevention, care, and treatment services. Testing strategies should utilize existing communityor health facility-based opportunities, such as antenatal clinics, HIV clinics, or tuberculosis (TB) clinics. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. Routine HBsAg testing is recommended for all pregnant women in antenatal clinics in settings with an HBsAg prevalence of ≥2% or ≥5%. This testing should also be linked to prevention, care, and treatment services. Couples and partners in antenatal care settings should be offered HBV testing services. This is a strong recommendation, albeit based on low-certainty evidence. Focused testing for HBV should be offered to individuals at higher risk, including adults and adolescents from populations with high HBV prevalence or those with a history of exposure or high-risk behaviors. This includes people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons, men who have sex with men, sex workers, people living with HIV, and close contacts of those with HBV infection. Testing should also be offered to individuals with clinical suspicion of chronic viral hepatitis, such as those with symptoms of liver disease, abnormal liver function tests, or unexplained liver disease. Health-care workers who have not been previously vaccinated should also be tested and vaccinated against HBV. Blood donors should be screened for HBV, with linkage to care, counseling, and treatment for those who test positive. For hepatitis C virus (HCV), serological testing for HCV antibodies is recommended for adults and adolescents from populations most affected by HCV, such as those with high HCV prevalence or a history of high-risk behaviors. Testing should also be offered to individuals with clinical suspicion of chronic viral hepatitis. Periodic retesting using HCV nucleic acid testing (NAT) should be considered for individuals with ongoing risk of HCV acquisition or reinfection. In settings with an HCV antibody prevalence of ≥2% or ≥5%, all adults should have access to HCV serological testing linked to prevention, care, and treatment services. Testing strategies should leverage existing communityor facility-based programs, such as HIV or TB clinics, drug treatment services, and antenatal clinics. Malaria remains a significant global health issue, causing high levels of morbidity and mortality. It is both preventable and treatable. According to the World Malaria Report, there were an estimated 220 million cases and 409,000 deaths globally in 2019. People living with HIV are at increased risk of severe malaria, depending on the intensity of malaria transmission in their area. Key interventions for malaria control include early diagnosis, prompt and effective treatment with artemisinin-based combination therapies, and the use of insecticide-treated nets and indoor residual spraying to control mosquito vectors. In areas of stable malaria transmission, people living with HIV should routinely use insecticide-treated bed nets or have access to indoor residual spraying to reduce their exposure to malaria. Intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy and seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis are recommended in areas of high transmission. However, sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine should not be given to people living with HIV or HIV-exposed infants who are taking co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Similarly, intermittent preventive treatment of malaria during pregnancy should not be provided in addition to co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. People living with HIV who develop malaria should receive prompt and effective antimalarial treatment. Parasitological confirmation of suspected malaria cases should be performed using microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests, but treatment should not be delayed if diagnostic confirmation is unavailable. Limited data exist on how HIV infection modifies therapeutic responses to artemisinin-based combination therapies. Early studies suggest that increasing HIV-related immunosuppression may be associated with decreased treatment response to antimalarial drugs. However, there is insufficient evidence to modify general malaria treatment recommendations for people living with HIV. For individuals with HIV and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, certain drug combinations should be avoided, such as artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine if they are on co-trimoxazole, or artesunate + amodiaquine if they are on efavirenz or zidovudine. Buruli ulcer, caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, is a neglected tropical disease primarily affecting poor populations in remote rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa. It is the third most common mycobacterial disease after tuberculosis and leprosy. Nearly half of those affected are children under 15 years of age. Areas endemic for Buruli ulcer often overlap with regions of high HIV prevalence. Preliminary evidence suggests that HIV infection may increase the risk of Buruli ulcer disease. Studies in Benin, Cameroon, and Ghana have shown that people with Buruli ulcer are 3–8 times more likely to be living with HIV than those without the disease. HIV may also affect the clinical presentation and severity of Buruli ulcer, with an increased incidence of larger and more ulcerated lesions among people living with HIV, particularly those with low CD4 cell counts. Buruli ulcer may occur in the context of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Diagnosis of Buruli ulcer in endemic areas can often be made clinically by experienced health-care workers. Molecular detection of M. ulcerans by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is used to confirm the diagnosis. If PCR is unavailable, other diagnostic methods, such as direct smear examination, histopathology, or culture, may be used. For ulcerative lesions, swabs should be taken from the undermined edges of the ulcer at the start of antibiotic treatment for direct smear examination, culture, and PCR. Swabs should also be taken at the end of antibiotic treatment if the lesion has not healed or if surgery is indicated.
